Senses.Explanation: “Whose house’s tune do you sing?” asks whose teaching lineage the person on the seat carries. Linji, Fenyang, Yangqi, and Hansong are each asked the same paired questions: whose house’s tune they sing and whose lineage style they inherit. The pairing makes “house” a teaching house and uses its “tune” for the style presently being voiced. The masters’ different replies show that the question has no fixed answer.

Entries.SourceTerm: 報化非真佛，亦非說法者

Senses.PreferredTarget: The reward and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speaker of the teaching
SearchAliases: the reward and transformation bodies are not the true buddha, nor are they the speaker of the teaching
Senses.Note: The line says that the reward and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha and are not the speaker of the teaching. Zhuanyu cites it while explaining why a Buddha image can still guide those who see it. Qianyan uses it to challenge a patron’s understanding of scripture, and Baiyu voices it before a Buddha hall. Liaotang places it beside the Buddha’s birth and sermons, asking what counts as the true Buddha. Jianfu warns students against mistaking even long cultivation for what the line points toward. Each use tests how forms and words work without making them final.

Senses.Explanation: An inherited line denies that a Buddha’s displayed bodies or speech alone are the true Buddha. Zhuanyu invokes it at a Buddha-image dedication; Qianyan applies it in a scripture colophon, and Baiyu speaks it before a Buddha hall. Liaotang asks whether the historical Buddha then taught at all; Jianfu uses the line to distinguish cultivation results from the matter sought.

Senses.Note: The formula is the back half of the couplet (貪觀白浪，失却手橈) and travels almost always as the pair; the front half has no entry of its own in the public termbase. The figure behind it is the ferryman who stares at the breakers and so drops the oar — attention spent on the spectacle forfeits the means of steering. Retained rows span eleven works from the tenth to the seventeenth century, with one lamp record kept for Baling's root answer.

Senses.Explanation: The formula (失却手橈, losing the oar in one's hands) is the back half of a boatman's warning (貪觀白浪，失却手橈 — greedy for gazing at the white waves, the oar is lost from the hands). Its oldest carrier is Baling Haojian, who answers a question about the patch-robed monk's own share with the couplet alone; Xuedou hangs it on Xuansha and Gushan when Gushan cannot say what Xuansha says; Kaifu Daoning calls Yantou's one turn of showing off greatly like it; and Muyun Tongmen turns it into a standing threat — lose the oar, and it is not merely wave-gazing: count on drowning in blind karma-consciousness. The answer class is the oldest. Baling Haojian's question-and-answer in the Jingde lamp record rules the tripitaka not a patch-robed monk's business, then answers what does fall to his share with the couplet alone; the bequest of his whisk closes the entry. Dongshan Shouchu answers the same way: asked why, if the ancestor came west transmitting one mind, every quarter teaches a different end, he answers with the couplet alone. Xuedou Chongxian, asked at the seat on his own Cuifeng mountain who the person in the scene is, after granting that those with eyes see the scene, answers the student with the couplet alone. Xuedou's verdict on the circle case became the formula's most-quoted form. Xuansha draws a circle when Gushan arrives; each says no one gets out of this; Gushan asks why Xuansha can say it and he cannot; Xuansha answers, I get it, you don't — and Xuedou rules: they only know how to gaze greedily at the white waves, they do not know they have lost the oar. Yuanwu Keqin's Beat-the-Rhythm record carries the same verdict by name into case eighty, with his own turn on Bei the ascetic's circle following it. Hongzhi Zhengjue's verdict on the Muzhou-Wuling exchange: Muzhou asks Wuling how the hair-tip swallows the great sea; Wuling deflects twice; neither takes up the words — and between the two of them, Hongzhi rules, someone is gazing at the white waves and has lost the oar, then holds up his whisk: look. Roughly three and a half centuries on, Wansong Xingxiu reprised the case for his own students in the Record of Requests: those who do not take up the words multiply by the day, and Tiantong — Hongzhi — would not let them off. Two verdicts on old cases of botched momentum. Kaifu Daoning on Yantou's sutra-office display — one turn of showing off, greatly like gazing at the white waves and losing the oar, while the silent scripture-keeper wins a move few in past or present know. Xutang Zhiyu on Yongquan seeing Xuefeng into his sedan chair: Yongquan, in the midstream of a perilous current, has lost the oar in his hands; Xuefeng's fault lies in his after-word — and had Xutang been there, he would have told him to ride the chair steadily, cutting Xuefeng's tongue and leaving no one in the world a needle's entry. Liao'an Qingyu works the formula three times in one record. On Yunmen's moon-in-the-water dialogue he rules that Yunmen's sword danced with an exit at every step, while the questioner gazed at the white waves and lost the oar; on the Luzu no-mouth exchange the same verdict on the questioner — and had he been a man, he would have overturned the seat; and on the very circle case Xuedou judged, he sets both sides down: say it or not, no one gets out of this — wave-gazing and oar-loss are idle words. Wansong's verdict on Luopu's submission to Jiashan: the two hold complementary registers — Luopu the gate-display, Jiashan the deep talk that enters the principle — and gazing at the white waves Luopu lost the oar and could not close the grip; the sour home-vinegar he had eaten told him, and he submitted. Muyun Tongmen warns the assembly at the circle case: say it if you can, and if you lose the oar it is not merely wave-gazing — count on the trackless flood of karma-consciousness. And Yunfeng Wenyue reads an old verse about racing dragon boats — once you have won a heat, you rest — as very much like gazing at the white waves and losing the oar, then dares the assembly: find the fault and save the old man, or the wheel of the teaching loses today.

Senses.Explanation: To rob the person on the spot is to seize what is present without first sending the victim elsewhere. Two compendia preserve one unsigned appraisal verse: ‘the question probes deep, the answer is still deeper; robbing the person on the spot is most free-flowing.’ Two recensions of Wuyi’s hall address form a second family: he joins the phrase to ‘borrowing the road to return home’ and to recognizing the immeasurable treasure-hoard immediately, making the robbery an image for taking the matter directly from present circumstances. In a third independent use, Pofeng answers the exchange in which Guishan turns Baizhang’s demand back on him with 就身打劫, judging Guishan’s reply an immediate seizure of the person questioning him. The records support immediacy and direct appropriation; they do not turn the phrase into a general doctrine of spiritual theft.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1416.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shuzhong Wuyun. Shuzhong Wuyun says the pair while offering incense for his teacher Zhuyuan. He calls the teacher a creditor and adversary, then retells how he asked about the dog's lack of Buddha nature, received a shout, and broke into a sweat. He presented a verse, only to be met with laughter and the question, 'How could that understanding do?' Shuzhong calls the second arrow deeper than the first. As he inserts the incense, even Boya's qin would hardly express his heart's melody. The line closes an account in which indebtedness and the sting of correction are deliberately spoken together; simple gratitude alone would leave out the passage's sharp language. The headword is rendered: Even with Boya's qin, one could hardly express what is in the heart. Here qin names a stringed zither.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB392.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hansong Cao. Hansong Zhicao uses it during incense offering at the raising of a beam for the memorial hermitage. He describes a bond deeper than father and son and an accord like ruler and minister, dedicating the offering to Baiyu Jingsi ten years after the teacher's death. The saying gives that bond more feeling than he claims he can voice, even with Boya's instrument. He then turns to pillars, rafters and beams fitting their places, with the teacher resting in the pagoda and monks inhabiting the hermitage. The line belongs to this enacted commemoration, not an abstract claim that music or words are always useless. The headword is rendered: Even with Boya's qin, one could hardly express what is in the heart. Here qin names a stringed zither.

Senses.Explanation: Unobstructed in every direction: the freedom the masters grant only at the point where dodging is impossible — and the last word more than one of them died saying. Jieweizhou Xingzhou, after the great furnace has melted the six senses into one and the eighty-four thousand pores shed light together, has them shoulder the whole thing and walk straight into a thousand peaks — eyes through the four great seas, feet kicking the five Sumerus, unobstructed at the crossroads of the singing quarter, roaming at will through the flute-and-song crowds; Feiyin Tongrong closes his verse answer with the decree — neither color nor sound, pointing straight at what is ready-made: when the glance-thought returns home the dust-burden drops, and being unblocked in every direction is itself the whole true — and then raises the old case of the monk who asked the nun of Mushan what Mushan is; Yinyuan Longqi rules it of the senses themselves: seeing color unmazed, hearing sound unbeguiled, touched by things unturned, burdened by the body unburdened — roots and fields laid out clear and unobstructed, so that one may sketch the natural truth on Brush-tip Peak and play the flute sideways on the sleeping ox; Minshu Ruxiang, forbidding his heirs to beg grave inscriptions from officials, gives his last verse — I am the king of the teaching, free in the teaching; coming and going free, unobstructed in every direction — and passes sitting cross-legged. Zhulang Chesheng plays the extremes against each other — plucking beard-hairs before the hungry tiger's cheeks, snatching food from under the hawk's claws: sometimes holding shut, and no news at all; sometimes letting run, and unobstructed in every direction — so, is it holding-shut, or letting-run? No one judges, so he footnotes it himself; Konggu Daocheng lifts his staff: this truth belongs to none of the five phases and takes no yin and yang — originally round and bright, unobstructed in every direction; grasp it here and beings are buddhas, miss it and buddhas are beings — understand or not, thirty blows either way; Tianyin Yuanxiu, raising the old meeting of Dongshan Liangjie and Yunju Daoying — the one with no road to come by, whom Dongshan said no thousand or ten thousand could hold — rules it the meeting of working masters: a pearl rolling in the bowl, a bowl rolling on the pearl, unobstructed in every direction, nothing like the lost-headed shadow-chaser chipping ice for fire; Zixian Jue, taking the room, lays down the three gates for whoever sits the curved-back chair: first, kill the buddhas and the founders leaving no trace; second, break the harmony of the assembly, unobstructed in every direction; third, in the pile of sights and sounds, walk, stand, sit, lie — and plants his staff: who will build it with me?

Yongjia Xuanjue's Song of Realizing the Way first recalls traveling over rivers and mountains to seek teachers, then says that recognizing the road of Caoxi made life and death no longer a binding concern. Walking and sitting, speaking and silence, movement and stillness are all described as inwardly at ease. The headword carries this into the hardest images: even blades do not disturb that composure, and even poison meets the same ease. The following verse invokes the teacher's earlier patient endurance and repeated lives and deaths, then says that awakening to the unborn leaves no grief or joy over honor and disgrace. The pair voices equanimity grounded in this realization, rather than a physical guarantee of immunity. Yongjia is the authored song's speaker; the surrounding first-person recollections belong to its poetic voice.

Wanru Tongwei says that Buddhas are ordinary people whose business is settled, while ordinary people are Buddhas whose business remains unsettled; a single turn of delusion or awakening makes the distinction. He raises Tianlong's lifted finger and Juzhi's recognition, and Niaoke's blown feather and Huitong's stopping, to insist on going directly to the root instead of pursuing branches. If one truly accords in this way, he says, one remains untroubled amid blades and at ease even with poison, without a thread hanging on the whole body. He then asks for a sentence that does not fall into ordinary feeling and answers with sages like a lightning flash and the vast world like bubbles in the sea. The inherited couplet has become Wanru's own present exhortation, conditional on actual accord; it does not offer a verbal formula that by itself produces fearlessness.

Suru Honghan asks a monk what conduct could reach the composure described by the blades-and-poison pair. The monk replies that when a foreigner comes a foreigner appears, and when a Chinese person comes a Chinese person appears. Suru asks what appears if neither comes. The monk says his house has no chart to identify such creatures, and no such strange apparitions. Asked how he has attained this, the monk answers that right and wrong do not reach the fisher's place, whereas honor and disgrace follow the rider on horseback. Suru says, 'Indeed.' The couplet is thus put forward by Suru as a present question about living practice, followed by specific replies and further testing. His assent belongs to that exchange; the record does not turn it into a universal explanation of every image in Yongjia's longer song.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase says the whole body of the matter stands openly present, leaving no hidden remainder for explanation to supply. Yuanwu Keqin places the phrase after freedom from being turned by words and before cutting off calculation in one stroke. When Jifei Ruyi tests his attendant Cui during his final illness, Cui answers the question ‘right at such a time, how is it?’ with this phrase and is pressed further. Chunbei Guangde calls the matter wholly manifest and without cover while warning against searching for it in books, talk, travel, or fixed staring; Yuechuang Liao says it is already wholly manifest before birth and contrasts it with the first stirring of a thought.

Senses.Explanation: Flourishing yellow flowers travels with the proposition that yellow flowers are wisdom, while the records preserve affirmation, rejection, and interview testing of that formula. The headword occurs 64 times across 45 files and the same number of works; the fuller yellow-flowers-and-wisdom formula occurs 24 times across 21 files and the same number of works. A question to National Teacher Huizhong reports disagreement over the proposition, and his answer accepts it by placing bamboo and flowers within the range of the teaching body and wisdom. A transmitted exchange then has Dazhu Huihai distinguish wisdom appearing in response to flowers from wisdom being located in the flowers. Yikui Yuankui rebukes people who hold rigidly to the formula, calling a fitting phrase a donkey-tethering stake, and elsewhere uses the flowers as a live examination question. The plant image therefore becomes a portable, disputed proposition rather than a single uncontested equation.

Senses.Explanation: Dahui raises a dispute over the old saying that luxuriant yellow flowers are nothing other than the perfection of wisdom: Nanyang Huizhong supports it, while Dazhu Huihai refuses to locate the perfection of wisdom inside the flowers themselves. Dahui Zonggao quotes an unnamed old worthy’s paired saying about green bamboo as the body of the teaching and yellow flowers as the perfection of wisdom. He then transmits Nanyang Huizhong’s scriptural defense and Dazhu Huihai’s reply that the perfection of wisdom appears in response to yellow flowers but is not an attribute possessed by the flowers. Dahui preserves the affirmation and the breaking-open together and tells students to see through both.
